comments.body:
🤖 **Corrected scope + consolidated repro. This is not a code regression, and the original title was wrong — I have retitled the issue.**

## Correction to the original report

The issue was filed as "regression since `5e496b051`" because that tree had completed 200 steps cleanly twice. That framing is **wrong**: `5e496b051` has since produced the same fault (`oldbaseB`, task 86, step 146). Both trees fail.

Also superseded from the original body: the leading hypothesis was #7951 (NCCL RAS polling). **That is exonerated** — `norasA` ran unmodified `main` with `NCCL_RAS_ENABLE=0` and still faulted. Checkpointing (#7929) is also not necessary: `ras8` faulted ~12 min in at step ~23, before any 30-minute checkpoint could exist.

Supporting the "not in this repo" conclusion: across `5e496b051..75d12bd05`, `model.py` and `heuristic.py` are unchanged, `launch.py` changes are confined to checkpointing/telemetry/watchdog, and **`uv.lock` is unchanged** — so the compiled program and the entire Python/CUDA toolchain are identical between the two trees.

## Full observation matrix

`II` = `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION`. All runs are 8 racks = 128 x GB200x4 = 512 GPUs on `cw-us-east-08a`, 200 steps requested.

| Tree | RAS | Local watchdog | Run | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `75d12bd05` | on | yes | `ras8` | **II** — task 80, step ~23 |
| `75d12bd05` | on | no *(pristine)* | `ctrl9` | **II** — task 5, step ~89 |
| `75d12bd05` | off | no *(pristine)* | `norasA` | **II** — task 13, step ~85 |
| `5e496b051` | on | yes | `oldbaseB` | **II** — task 86, step 146 |
| `5e496b051` | on | no *(pristine)* | `oldpureD` | **wedge**, no error (#7344) — step 189 |
| `5e496b051` | on | no | `repro-v3` *(prev. day)* | **wedge**, no error (#7344) — step 182 |
| `5e496b051` | on | no | `obs`, `obs4` *(prev. day)* | clean, 200 steps, x2 |

Every II is from 2026-08-04. The previous day's four runs on `5e496b051` produced one wedge and two clean 200-step runs and **zero** IIs.

**Relationship to #7344 is unresolved.** The signatures are clearly different (II is loud, single-rank, kills the gang; the wedge is silent, all-ranks, hangs indefinitely with zero `CUDA_ERROR` in the full log range). But a single underlying GPU fault that sometimes raises an error and sometimes just stops progressing would explain both, and an II *does* produce a wedge-like downstream state — `oldbaseB`'s RAS snapshot showed one rack lagging with every rank alive and nothing marked dead. I am not claiming these are independent bugs.

## The error

```
jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: INTERNAL: Failed to retrieve branch_index value on stream 0x…:
  CUDA error: Could not synchronize CUDA stream:
  CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION: an illegal instruction was encountered
```

CUDA errors are asynchronous, so the `branch_index` site is only where JAX noticed a poisoned context — the illegal instruction executed in an earlier kernel.

## Environment

Observed on-node, from an NCCL RAS report captured on a live training rank:

```
nccl_version          2.28.9
cuda_driver_version   13020      (CUDA 13.2 driver API)
cuda_runtime_version  13000      (CUDA 13.0 runtime)
```

Pinned in `uv.lock`, identical on both trees:

```
jax / jaxlib          0.11.0        nvidia-nccl-cu13    2.28.9
jax-cuda13-plugin     0.11.0        nvidia-cudnn-cu13   9.19.0.56
jax-cuda13-pjrt       0.11.0        triton              3.6.0
```

Hardware: `cw-us-east-08a`, `gb200-4x` nodes (2x Grace Arm v9, 144 vCPU, 960 GB LPDDR5X, 4x Blackwell), `multinode-nvlink-ib`, gang-scheduled.

## Still missing — and I cannot obtain it

**The kernel-mode NVIDIA driver version (`580.xx`-style) is not recorded anywhere I can reach.** `cuda_driver_version 13020` above is the CUDA driver *API* version, which is not the same thing. I checked `iris.worker` telemetry — it carries `gpu_power_w`, `gpu_temp_c`, `gpu_util_pct`, `hbm_*`, but no driver identity — and `iris process` has no exec, so I cannot run `nvidia-smi` on a node.

This is the single most valuable missing field, because the strongest evidence here is temporal: the same commit ran clean one day and fails the next with an unchanged toolchain. Anyone with node access can settle it with:

```bash
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version,vbios_version --format=csv
```

Two other useful items in the same vein:

1. **Xid / DCGM at the four fault timestamps below.** An illegal instruction normally raises a driver Xid (13 / 31 / 43 class). A shared Xid across four different physical nodes separates a fleet or driver problem from a generated-kernel fault, and costs no GPU time.
2. **Node image / firmware version history for `cw-us-east-08a`** covering 2026-08-03 ~16:00 UTC → 2026-08-04 ~06:30 UTC, the window between the last clean run and the first failure.

## Fault coordinates

All 2026-08-04 UTC. First `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` line for the attempt.

| Run | Tree | First fault | Task | Node |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ras8` | `75d12bd05` | 06:50:24 | 80 | `s38vxs64` |
| `ctrl9` | `75d12bd05` | 08:21:16 | 5 | `s6xvxs64` |
| `norasA` | `75d12bd05` | 14:27:16 | 13 | (not captured) |
| `oldbaseB` | `5e496b051` | 15:28:11 | 86 | (rack 5; RAS shows subnet `10.186.210.0/24` lagging) |

## Reproduce

```bash
RID=<run-id>
git checkout 75d12bd05   # or 5e496b051 — both reproduce
iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --enable-extra-resources \
  --target-cluster cw-us-east-08a --priority production \
  --cpu 2 --memory 8GB --disk 32GB --timeout 21600 \
  --job-name "${RID}-coord" -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" \
  -- python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_fsdp.launch \
     --run-id "$RID" --dp-racks 8 --num-steps 200 --version dev --run
```

`--target-cluster cw-us-east-08a` is required — Iris child jobs inherit the parent's region, so without it the GB200 request is pinned to wherever the coordinator landed and returns `unschedulable: no scaling group provides device gpu:gb200`.

Retrieve the fault with `--since-ms` timestamp windows, not `--tail`: during the failure the 128 tasks emit ~15k lines/sec, so the crash is displaced from even a 40,000-line tail within seconds.

**Expected detection power.** Fitting a constant per-step hazard to the three main-tree faults gives `p ≈ 0.015/step`, so a 200-step run has roughly a **95%** chance of surfacing this (95% CI on the required length is wide: 66–950 steps). A single clean 200-step run is therefore reasonable but not conclusive evidence of a fix.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Fleet is fully homogeneous — the "cluster changed underneath us" theory is not supported. But the fault rate does differ by tree, so my previous "not a code regression" retitle was also too strong. Both corrected below.**

## Kernel-mode driver version (the field that was missing)

Obtained from CoreWeave node labels via the cluster kubeconfig — no exec required:

```bash
kubectl --kubeconfig ~/.kube/coreweave-iris --context marin-us-east-08a_US-EAST-08A get nodes -o json
```

Across **all 205 GB200 nodes in `cw-us-east-08a`**, every version dimension is identical:

```
kernel                    6.17.13-155-gdec5393c-coreweave-arm64
OS                        Ubuntu 24.04
GPU driver                595.71.05
GPU firmware (all 4)      97.00.B9.00.99
Mellanox NIC fw (all 4)   28.47.2526
ncore image               2.49.0  /  ofed-d30da48-n595-kver6.17-gdec5393c-bundle-arm64
CUDA driver API           13020        CUDA runtime  13000
NCCL                      2.28.9
```

(The only 4 non-GB200 nodes in the cluster are CPU-class; they carry no GPU labels and are unrelated.)

## This undercuts the fleet-change hypothesis

I previously argued the regression was likely a node image / driver / firmware change, because the same commit ran clean on 2026-08-03 and failed on 2026-08-04 with `uv.lock` unchanged. The node labels do not support that:

- **Zero heterogeneity** — one kernel, one driver, one GPU firmware, one NIC firmware, one node image across the entire GB200 fleet.
- The nodes that actually faulted have carried this driver **since their creation in July**: `s38vxs64` created 2026-07-15, `s6xvxs64` created 2026-07-25, `s1nrxs64` created 2026-07-22. Their `nvidia.com/gfd.timestamp` equals their creation time, i.e. the GPU labels were never refreshed by a driver upgrade.
- 16 GB200 nodes *were* created 2026-08-04 13:17–13:28 UTC, but they are autoscaler capacity with **identical** images, and they postdate the first two faults (06:50 and 08:21 UTC).

So unless a driver was swapped in place without the GPU Operator relabelling — which would be unusual — the fleet did not change between the clean runs and the failing ones.

## Correcting my own retitle: the rate does differ by tree

I retitled this issue "not a code regression" on the strength of `5e496b051` also faulting. Looking at rates rather than presence/absence, that was too strong:

| Tree | II events | Exposed steps | rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| `75d12bd05` | 3 | 197 | 0.0152 / step |
| `5e496b051` | 1 | 917 | 0.0011 / step |

**Rate ratio ≈ 14x.** Under a null of equal rates, main would be expected to produce 0.71 events and produced 3; one-sided Poisson gives **p ≈ 0.035**. That is marginal evidence, not proof, but it is enough that a code contribution should not be dismissed.

Exposure accounting: main = the three II runs; old tree = `oldbaseB` (II at 146) plus `oldpureD` (189, wedged), `repro-v3` (182, wedged), `obs` and `obs4` (200 each, clean) as censored observations.

**Caveats, which are substantial at 3 vs 1 events:**

1. Small numbers. The confidence interval on a 14x ratio with four total events is very wide.
2. **Tree and time-of-day are partly confounded.** The main-tree runs are mostly early (06:50, 08:21) and the old-tree runs are late (15:28, 16:47), with `norasA` at 14:27 in between. If anything drifted across the day, it is aliased onto the tree comparison.
3. The old-tree exposure includes the previous day's runs, when conditions may not have been identical.

## Where that leaves it

- The fault is **real on both trees** — a bisect that assumes `5e496b051` is clean will mislead.
- Main is **plausibly much worse**, so the 15-commit range is worth revisiting rather than dismissed. Given `model.py`, `heuristic.py`, and `uv.lock` are all unchanged across it, the mechanism would have to be indirect — scheduling/placement (#7928 makes CPU reservations topology-aware on CoreWeave, which can change NUMA and device affinity) is the most plausible candidate remaining.
- Distinguishing a 14x rate difference from noise needs roughly **4-5 more runs per arm**, which is expensive; the cheaper discriminator is still Xid/DCGM at the four fault timestamps already listed in this issue.

Correcting the title accordingly to reflect both trees and the rate difference.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## New instance with full all-rank verification: `moe-hero-fsdp-12rack-r25fa4-20260805`

Hit this while running the #7344 ablation ladder. This capture is cleaner than earlier ones
because it brackets the onset exactly rather than post-kill flood — see the capture note at
the bottom.

**Config:** 12 racks (192 nodes / 768 GPUs), `num_layers=1`, `attention_implementation="gpu_fa4_cute"`,
`moe_implementation="sonic_cute"`, `expert_chunks=4`, real data, `offload_opt_state=False`.

### Timeline (cluster time)

| time | rank | event |
|---|---|---|
| 06:01:20 | **all 0–191** | step **300**, loss 4.74, ~1.2 s/step — uniformly healthy |
| 06:01:21.433359 | **78** | `cudaFreeAsync failed to free …: CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` |
| →06:01:22.104668 | 78 | 666 failed `cudaFreeAsync` + 19 failed module unloads = 685 lines, devices [0]–[3] |
| 06:06:22.998317 | 0 | `Shutdown barrier … DEADLINE_EXCEEDED … 1/192 … first task at the barrier: 78` |
| 06:06:23.007 | all | `Terminating process because the JAX distributed service detected fatal errors` |

### All-rank verification

A single bounded query against the training-job parent from 06:01:15 with
`--no-tail --max-lines 100000`, grouped by task, shows:

- step 300 logged by **every** task 0–191;
- **no** task logged step 301;
- all 685 illegal-instruction records came from **task 78 only**;
- no other task produced any CUDA error.

So task 78 is the first and only *logged* GPU fault in the complete retrievable onset window.
(An unreported lower-level failure elsewhere can't be excluded from logs alone.)

### The 300 s is JAX's default shutdown timeout

Last teardown error → barrier expiry = **300.894 s**, which is JAX's default
`shutdown_timeout_seconds=300`. The gang did not hang indefinitely; it waited exactly one
shutdown timeout and aborted.

This gives a **discriminator against #7344**: a #7956 fault self-aborts within ~300 s,
whereas #7344 runs sit with `failures=0` and all tasks alive for far longer (measured:
4883 s, 5590 s, 7203 s). I'd suggest keeping the two issues separate on that basis, while
leaving open that they could share a root cause.

### Notes on attribution

- `cudaFreeAsync` is only where the **sticky, asynchronous** error surfaced — not the
  offending kernel. This capture lacks the explicit `JaxRuntimeError … Failed to retrieve
  branch_index … [executable_name='jit_train_step']` seen in earlier occurrences.
- Allocator `InUse` was 55.20 GiB against a 138.22 GiB limit — **no memory pressure**.
- `InUse` then falls 55.20 → 3.55 GiB → 65 MiB alongside the errors and module unloads:
  an unwind/teardown pattern.
- Errors appear on devices [0]–[3], but that does **not** establish propagation from one
  device — the same executable runs on all four.
- The same executable ran successfully for ~300 steps and has failed on varying ranks across
  occurrences. That argues against a plain architecture/SASS target mismatch and toward a
  data-dependent kernel bug, memory corruption, or a driver/hardware fault.

### Suggested next step

The most informative single run is `moe_implementation="scatter"` **with
`expert_chunks=1`** (required — `_moe/local.py:64` rejects `scatter`/`sonic` unless
`expert_chunks == 1`, so neither is a one-field swap), everything else unchanged. That gives
a stock-XLA MoE control, removing the QuACK/CUTLASS grouped GEMMs.

Worth noting for anyone testing the toolchain: `sonic_cute` depends on `quack-kernels==0.6.1`
and `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.6.0`. A NCCL/cuDNN/Triton bump does **not** update those primary
kernel packages.

Highest-value no-GPU action first: correlate node/Xid/DCGM data for task 78 at 06:01:21.433.

### Capture procedure

`iris job logs <TASK path> --level info --since-seconds N --no-tail`

`--no-tail` combined with `--since` returns the **earliest** lines in the window, so it
reaches the fault onset. Plain `--tail` returns the most recent lines, which after a kill or
auto-retry is pure shutdown/setup flood — several of my earlier captures spanned a single
second and were no evidence at all. Also note `--level error` is dominated by `uv` install
output on restart, since uv writes to stderr.

🤖 Filed while investigating #7344; analysis independently reviewed before posting.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Node/rack table for all 7 known occurrences, a repeat offender, and a confound that blocks attribution

Two more occurrences today, plus recovered node identities for every earlier one.
**Correction first:** the "first fault 15:28:11" in this issue's body is wrong — that is a
healthy step-137 timestamp. The first retained illegal-instruction record for `oldbaseB` is
**2026-08-04 15:31:32.844856 UTC** on `s7htxs64`.

### All known occurrences with node identity

Recovered by joining Iris's retained `task_attempts.node_name` against the node inventory:

| run | rank | node / IP | physical rack | mesh position |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| `ctrl9` | 5 | `s6xvxs64` / `10.186.213.49` | r392 | replica 0, data 20–23 |
| `norasA` | 13 | `sj1txs64` / `10.186.213.67` | r392 | replica 0, data 52–55 |
| `oldbaseB` | 86 | `s7htxs64` / `10.186.210.235` | r129 | replica 5, data 24–27 |
| `ras8` | 80 | `s38vxs64` / `10.186.210.229` | r129 | replica 5, data 0–3 |
| `rasB` | 136 | `s9xvxs64` / `10.186.210.195` | r128 | replica 8, data 32–35 |
| `r25fa4` | 78 | `sjwsxs64` / `10.186.207.87` | **r122** | replica 4, data 56–59 |
| `r3nopgle` | 75 | `sgd50t64` / `10.186.207.109` | **r122** | replica 4, data 44–47 |

**All seven fault nodes are distinct.** Rack counts: r392=2, r129=2, r128=1, r122=2. So there
is no single universally-bad rack across history — but several two-event rack/mesh pairs.

### A repeat offender within one job

`moe-hero-fsdp-12rack-r3nopgle-20260805` died twice, and **rank 75 (`sgd50t64`) is implicated
in both**:

- crash 1 (step 7): 4902 `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` lines, **all from rank 75**
- crash 2 (step 110): `Shutdown barrier … 1/192`, **first task at the barrier: 75** (no
  illegal-instruction record inside the captured window)

Iris reuses the same allocation across retries, so this is the same physical node twice.

### The confound that blocks attribution

`r25fa4` and `r3nopgle` used **the identical 192 nodes at identical task indices**. And the
mesh is built by reshaping global `jax.devices()` straight into
`(replica_dcn, data, expert, model)` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/sharding.py:168`), so
with 1 process × 4 GPUs per task:

```
replica_dcn = rank // 16
```

**Ranks 64–79 are simultaneously the whole physical r122 slice AND the entire logical
`replica_dcn=4` slice.** The scheduler makes 16-rank topology slices contiguous by task
ordinal (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py:931`), and its rack ordering was
stable, so replica 4 repeatedly landed on r122.

That matters because batches are sharded over `("replica_dcn", "data", "expert")` and the
loader selects examples from the device sharding map
(`lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/loader.py:202`) — **replica 4 sees different examples and
different MoE routing than other replicas.** A data-dependent kernel bug and a bad rack are
currently indistinguishable. (The two faults did occupy different `data` quartets, so it is
at least not one exact repeated data coordinate.)

I found no special-casing of ranks 64–79 or replica 4 in the code; only rank 0 is the JAX
coordinator, and the compiled SPMD program is symmetric across `replica_dcn`.

### On the statistics — I want to be explicit that these are weak

I initially computed `(16/192)² = 0.7%`. **That is the wrong reference class**: it assumes the
rack was named before either fault. Honest numbers:

- same rack, *after* the first fault identified r122: **1/12 = 8.3%**
- any rack collecting ≥2 of the three 12-rack faults (r128, r122, r122): **23.6%**
- same `/24` collision, using the actual unequal subnet sizes: **31.9%**

And the two runs are not independent allocation trials — same fleet, same rank mapping. So:
**suggestive operational signal, weak statistical evidence.** It justifies telemetry and a
provisional quarantine, not a declaration that r122 is bad.

### Asks

1. **Xid / DCGM telemetry** at the seven node/timestamp coordinates above — per-GPU Xids,
   SXid/NVLink errors, ECC, row-remap/retired pages, resets, DCGM diagnostics. This is the
   most perishable evidence and the highest-value next step. Application logs contain no Xid
   or DCGM records, so this has to come from the fleet side.
2. **Either** temporarily quarantine `DH1-122-US-EAST-08A`, **or** rotate the
   topology-domain ordering so `replica_dcn=4` lands on different hardware. The rotation is
   the better experiment: it de-aliases rack from mesh position. If the fault follows
   replica 4 to new hardware, the hardware theory dies.

There appears to be no user-facing placement/exclusion control for this: `ResourceConfig`
exposes region/zone/cluster/device but not rack or node
(`lib/fray/src/fray/types.py:413`), and while the Iris protobuf can express `NE`, the K8s
backend only translates `EQ` for known `pool`/`region` keys — rack is not mapped
(`.../k8s/tasks.py:306`). So this needs cluster ops.

### Impact on the #7344 ladder

A #7956 crash is a **competing risk** that right-censors an ablation rung — it is not
evidence the rung does or does not wedge. Two rungs in a row have now been censored (rung 2.5
at step 300, rung 3 at steps 7 and 110), so I am pausing advancement to later rungs rather
than reading censored runs as results.

🤖 Node identities recovered and statistics corrected via independent review.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Correction to my previous comment: `moe_implementation="scatter"` has already been tested

In [my earlier comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5188810589) I
proposed `moe_implementation="scatter"` + `expert_chunks=1` as the "most informative single
run", on the premise that the QuACK/CUTLASS MoE path had never been ablated.

**That premise was wrong.** It was ablated, in rung 1 of the #7344 ladder. Provenance from
that run:

```
[provenance] model: num_layers=1 attn=reference moe=scatter expert_chunks=1 sconv=True rope_fused=True vocab=128256 seq=4096
```

So the suggested "control" configuration has already run — and it **wedged** (#7344, step 78,
twice). I asserted it was untested by reading the current working-tree config instead of the
provenance line, which is exactly what that line exists to prevent.

### What the existing data does and does not say

**For #7344 (the wedge):** both vendored CuTe families are already excluded as *necessary*
causes — the wedge reproduces with `attn=reference` **and** `moe=scatter`.

**For #7956 (this issue):** the run is still weakly informative, because the endpoints differ.
Every illegal-instruction fault observed so far occurred with `gpu_fa4_cute` + `sonic_cute`
active; none has been seen under `reference` + `scatter`:

| config | II faults | note |
|---|---|---|
| `gpu_fa4_cute` + `sonic_cute` | 7 occurrences | ctrl9, norasA, oldbaseB, ras8, rasB, r25fa4, r3nopgle |
| `reference` + `scatter` | 0 | r1recap, l1, l1b, r1stockb |

But those rung-1 runs accumulated only a few hundred steps before wedging, so at the observed
fault rate the expected count is order-1. **Absence there is suggestive, not exculpatory**, and
I should not have implied a clean control existed either way.

### Revised suggestion

A dedicated `reference` + `scatter` run held to a pre-declared exposure would make that row
meaningful, but it is expensive and the wedge will keep ending the runs early. The better
target is the un-ablated remainder — **`sconv=True` and `rope_fused=True` were active in rung 1**
and have never been varied in any run.

Separately, `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` appears to **suppress** the fault rather than localise it
(0 faults in 1185 steps vs 3 in 417 without it), so it cannot serve as an attribution tool
here. Explicit synchronisation boundaries around attention / MoE / loss / optimizer — the other
half of @rjpower's [suggestion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5181330482)
— preserve kernel overlap and remain the more promising route.

🤖 Correcting my own error rather than leaving a wrong premise in the thread.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Five more faults today at 4 racks with `sonic_cute`, with reconstructed coordinates for @ClassicLarry's report above.**

Following up on [larry's report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5246921481). I pulled the retained Iris attempt records and logs for both `mhep-ctxext-d2048-fsdp-chunk4-to-fsdp-chunk1` jobs: five distinct single-rank faults, four of them consecutive attempts of one job.

Config, read from the W&B run config rather than a working tree:

```
attention_implementation  gpu_fa4_cute     moe_implementation  sonic_cute
expert_chunks             1                capacity_factor     1.0
hidden_dim 2048   num_layers 22   num_experts 128   top-k 4   num_shared_experts 2
max_seq_len 65536   sliding_window 2048
replica_axis_size 4   expert_axis_size 1   train_batch_size 256  (16.8M tokens/step)
offload_opt_state False   enable_pgle False
```

## Fault coordinates

Onset is the first `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` line of the attempt. Every event is single-rank: no other task emitted a CUDA error anywhere in the window.

| Job | Attempt | Onset (UTC) | Rank | Node | Attempt ended |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `…-20260810` | 0 | 17:05:12 | 14 | `sgzvxs64` | 17:10:25 |
| `…-20260810b` | 0 | 17:46:57 | 2 | `s5trxs64` | 17:52:09 |
| `…-20260810b` | 1 | 18:13:31 | 2 | `s5trxs64` | 18:18:47 |
| `…-20260810b` | 2 | 18:57:01 | 2 | `s5trxs64` | 19:02:15 |
| `…-20260810b` | 3 | 19:18:35 | 4 | `s8rrxs64` | killed by user |

The 300 s mechanism reproduces exactly. Attempt 0's fault at 17:46:57 produced `Shutdown barrier in coordination service has failed … The first task at the barrier: 2` at 17:51:59, 302 s later. The teardown shape matches too — the 19:18:35 event emitted 2481 `failed to unload module`, 920 `cudaFreeAsync`, and 132 `Error destroying CUDA event` lines in under a second, all from the one rank.

## Three corrections to the reproduction section

**4 racks reproduce it.** Every prior event was 8 or 12 racks. At 256 GPUs this is a third the cost of the 8-rack recipe currently in the description.

**`expert_chunks=1` reproduces it.** All nine prior faults ran `expert_chunks=4`, so chunking is not necessary.

**The model shape is not load-bearing.** d2048 / 22 layers / seq 65536 faults the same way as the hero's d6144 / 48 layers / seq 4096.

The hazard is also much higher here than the ~0.015/step the body fits: four consecutive attempts, each dying after 100–500 steps.

## A trap for anyone building the Xid table

In none of the four attempts does the Iris-recorded failed task match the faulting rank. Iris marks rank 0 (`exit_code 133`, node `s1wvxs64`) in three of them and rank 13 in the fourth; those are the coordinator and a barrier casualty, not the rank that executed the illegal instruction. The faulting ranks — 14, 2, 2, 4 — come only from the logs. Correlating Xid against the `task_attempts.state=5` node would point at the wrong hardware.

## Repeat offender, with the usual confound

`s5trxs64` faulted three consecutive times. Attempts 0–2 reused one allocation, so rank 2 and `s5trxs64` are perfectly confounded — the same aliasing described in [this comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5188810589). Attempt 3 drew a fresh allocation and faulted on rank 4 on a different node, so the fault did not follow mesh position 2 onto new hardware. That is one observation, and it points away from a purely data-dependent explanation.

## Concurrent control without `sonic_cute`

`mhep-hero-d6144-sw2048-20T-10r-watch-20260810` ran on the same fleet in the same window: 10 racks / 640 GPUs, `gpu_fa4_cute` with `moe_implementation="fixed_all_to_all"`, 48 layers, d6144. Clean past step 175 and still running. An earlier 640-GPU run of the same family reached step 435 before larry killed it, also clean. Neither emitted the signature.

That exposure is far too small to clear the FA4 path — at the historical rate the expected count is order-1, the same objection that applies to the rung-1 rows. It is worth recording only because it is the FA4-without-`sonic_cute` path running clean on the same cluster, on the same day, while every `sonic_cute` attempt faulted.

## Capture recipe

`iris query "SELECT task_id, attempt_id, state, node_name FROM task_attempts WHERE task_id LIKE '…'"` recovers per-attempt `node_name` from the controller DB with no cluster access, including for attempts that were later killed. For logs, `--no-tail --since-ms <onset minus 60s>` reaches the onset; the fault emits ~3.5k error lines in well under a second, so `--tail` misses it, and a window that starts before training begins fills the line cap with `uv` install output on stderr.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **This reproduces on 1 rack / 64 GPUs. The 8-rack recipe in the description is 8x larger than it needs to be.**

Building on the 4-rack `ctxext` faults [above](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5247127430), I ran that shape down the rack ladder. It faulted at one rack, with `replica_axis_size=1`.

```
[rank0] E0811 02:30:45.245461  cuda_event.cc:50] CUDA error: Error destroying CUDA event:
        CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION: an illegal instruction was encountered
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Run | `ii-repro-1rack-b-20260811-0215` (W&B `marin-community/marin_moe`) |
| Shape | 1 rack, 16 nodes, **64 GPUs**, `replica_axis_size=1`, `expert_axis_size=1` |
| Onset | 2026-08-11 02:30:45.245 UTC, ~36 s after the first step, before step 1 was logged |
| Faulting rank | iris task 14, local rank 0 = global JAX rank 56, node `sg8txs64` |
| Signature | 3473 lines: 2393 `failed to unload module`, 664 `cudaFreeAsync`, 399 CUDA-event destroys, 17 host-memory unregisters |
| Isolation | only task 14 emitted any CUDA error; the other 15 tasks were clean |
| Gang death | `local rank 0 exited with code -6` at 02:35:50 — **305 s** after onset |
| Final state | `failures=1`, `failed=1`, `cosched_failed=15` |

Same mechanism as every prior occurrence, at an eighth of the hardware: one rank takes a device-side
fault, its context is destroyed, it reaches the shutdown barrier alone, and one 300 s JAX timeout
later the gang dies.

## What this retires

At `replica_axis_size=1` there are no cross-rack DCN collectives in the program at all. The
multi-rack explanations in this thread cannot be the mechanism:

- the r122 quarantine proposal and the "one bad rack" framing;
- the `replica_dcn=4` / rank-64-79 mesh aliasing described in
  [this comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5188810589);
- the `s5trxs64` repeat-offender confound from the 4-rack runs;
- the 16-rank topology-slice reasoning behind all of the above.

A per-node hardware story is not excluded — `sg8txs64` also held a task in an earlier preempted
attempt — but it is no longer needed to explain anything.

## Reproduce

Model shape, from the faulting 4-rack `ctxext` W&B config, on `main` at `d7bddb0ad`:

```
hidden_dim 2048   num_layers 22   num_experts 128   top-k 4   num_shared_experts 2
num_heads 16   num_kv_heads 4   head_dim 128   intermediate_dim 1024
max_seq_len 65536   sliding_window 2048   capacity_factor 1.0
gpu_fa4_cute + sonic_cute   expert_chunks 1
1 rack, batch 64 -> 4.19M tokens/step
```

`main` has no launcher for this shape; I added it as a `--variant ctxext` on the FSDP hero launcher
(a config builder plus a CLI choice) and plumbed `max_task_failures` through
`dispatch_grug_training_run`, which hardcoded 10. Say the word if that is worth a PR rather than a
local branch.

```bash
RID=ii-repro-1rack-$(date -u +%Y%m%d-%H%M)
uv run --frozen iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --enable-extra-resources \
  --target-cluster cw-us-east-08a --priority production \
  --cpu 2 --memory 8GB --disk 32GB --timeout 86400 \
  --job-name "${RID}-coord" -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" -e JAX_ENABLE_PGLE 0 \
  -- python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_fsdp.launch \
     --run-id "$RID" --dp-racks 1 --batch-size 64 --num-steps 500 \
     --variant ctxext --mode stock-control --no-save-checkpoints --version dev --run
```

`--mode stock-control` runs the plain entrypoint with `max_retries_failure=0`, so the faulting
attempt survives for inspection instead of warm-restarting from step 1.

**`-e JAX_ENABLE_PGLE 0` is required, and cost me two attempts to learn.** `HERO_FSDP_RUNTIME_ENV`
defaults `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=1`; at this config that dies 28 s into training with
`jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: ALREADY_EXISTS: Another profiling session active` in `train_step`, then
takes the gang on the same 300 s barrier and looks superficially like this issue. The faulting
`ctxext` runs had `enable_pgle: false`, so PGLE off is also the more faithful setting.

## Two traps for anyone reading these logs

**`CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED` is not this issue.** The PGLE crash above produced 674 lines of
`cudaFreeAsync failed to free ...: CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED: Invalid access of peer GPU memory over
nvlink`, single-rank, with the same allocator stats dump. It is teardown fallout: those lines are
timestamped *after* the barrier failure, whereas a real occurrence precedes it. Check the ordering
against the barrier, not the shape of the flood.

**The rate is low and this is not a reliable reproducer.** The same config on the same rack ran 500
steps clean an hour earlier (`ii-repro-1rack-20260811-0105`, 3.7 s/it), so it is 1 fault in 2 valid
attempts. Two earlier attempts were censored, one by preemption at step 163 and one by the PGLE
crash. Budget several runs.

## Control

`mhep-hero-d6144-sw2048-20T-10r-watch-20260810` ran on the same cluster across the same window:
10 racks, 640 GPUs, `gpu_fa4_cute` with `moe_implementation="fixed_all_to_all"`, 48 layers, d6144.
It reached step ~999 over ~14.2 h and was then killed by its owner, with zero signature at any point
(polled every 5 minutes for the whole run). That is roughly 9,000 GPU-hours of FA4 exposure without
`sonic_cute` and no fault, against a 64-GPU `sonic_cute` job that faulted 36 s in.

The low-exposure objection that applies to the rung-1 rows does not apply to that control. It is
still not a controlled comparison — model shape, sequence length, MoE kernel, and batch all differ
at once — and it ended by a kill rather than a fixed budget, so it does not settle `sonic_cute`.

## Divergences from the faulting 4-rack config

Recorded so nobody reads this as an exact transcription: `offload_opt_state=True` here versus
`False` there (the hero trainer sets it), and `qb_estimator` does not exist on `main` so
`qb_estimator=HIST` is not reproduced. Everything the `main` model config can express matches.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Both of my 1-rack faults landed on the same GPU: `sg8txs64` device 0. Every run that did not draw that node ran clean.**

Second 1-rack reproduction, and this one carries the canonical error from the issue title, which my [first 1-rack fault](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5256188981) did not show:

```
jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: INTERNAL: Failed to retrieve branch_index value on stream 0xb20bc6e3b350:
  CUDA error: Could not synchronize CUDA stream:
  CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION: an illegal instruction was encountered
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Run | `ii-unarmed-1rack-20260811-1900` |
| Onset | 2026-08-11 20:15:57.114 UTC, step ~166 |
| Faulting rank | iris task 14, local rank 0, **node `sg8txs64`** |
| Signature | 4166 lines, single rank; no other task emitted a CUDA error |
| Gang death | abort at 20:21:03, `failures=1`, `cosched_failed=15` |

## The node table

Eleven 1-rack runs of the same `ctxext` config, over 21 hours. `sg8txs64` is the only node that
distinguishes the faults from the clean runs.

| Run | `sg8txs64` in allocation | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `ii-repro-1rack-20260811-0105` | yes, task 14 | clean, 500/500 |
| `ii-repro-1rack-b-20260811-0215` | yes, task 14 | **fault on task 14** |
| `ii-unarmed-1rack-20260811-1900` | yes, task 14 | **fault on task 14** |
| `ii-repro-1rack-20260810-2335` | yes, task 13 | preempted — censored |
| `ii-repro-1rack-20260811-0020` | yes, task 14 | crashed on a PGLE profiling collision — censored |
| `ii-ctrl-scatter-1rack-20260811-1501` | no | clean, 500/500 |
| `ii-repro-1rack-dump-20260811-1500` | no | clean, 500/500 |
| `ii-dump-1rack-{a,b,c,d}-20260811` | no | clean, 500/500 each |

Both faults are the same node **and** the same device index on it. Fisher exact on the six valid
runs without the node (0 faults) against the three with it (2 faults) gives p ≈ 0.08.

## Why this is not "found the bad GPU"

- **The node is not sufficient.** `ii-repro-1rack-20260811-0105` ran 500 clean steps with
  `sg8txs64` as task 14. Something else has to coincide.
- **The fleet history contradicts a single bad device.** Faults in this thread have been recorded on
  at least ten distinct nodes — `sgzvxs64`, `s5trxs64`, `s8rrxs64`, `s38vxs64`, `s6xvxs64`,
  `sj1txs64`, `s7htxs64`, `s9xvxs64`, `sjwsxs64`, `sgd50t64`. One defective GPU cannot explain those.

What it is consistent with is a population of *marginal* devices, with a small 1-rack draw pool
repeatedly returning one of them. That moves "a GPU or driver-level fault not visible in node
labels" — open hypothesis 1 in the description — back up the ranking, and it makes the Xid
correlation this issue has wanted much more targeted: **two exact timestamps on one named node**,
02:30:45.245 and 20:15:57.114 UTC on 2026-08-11, both `sg8txs64`, both device 0.

## A confound worth publishing, because I nearly reported the opposite

I had been running attempts with CUDA device core dumps armed
(`CUDA_ENABLE_COREDUMP_ON_EXCEPTION=1`), and the armed runs went 0 faults in 5 while unarmed went 2
in 3. Given that `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` is already known to suppress this fault, instrumentation
suppressing it was a live reading, and I was about to treat it as one.

It was allocation, not instrumentation: **all five armed runs happened to draw node sets without
`sg8txs64`**, because the node was held by another job for that whole window. Anyone comparing fault
rates across runs here should check node membership before attributing a difference to a knob.

## Still no core dump

A dump only gets written when a device exception occurs, and the two exceptions both landed on
unarmed runs — one predating the tooling, one the deliberate unarmed control. Five armed runs, two
faults, never the same run.

The arming and capture path is verified working end to end (uploader confirmed active on every rank,
writing to the run's output prefix); it has simply never been present at the moment of a fault. Iris
exposes no node-level placement constraint — `ResourceConfig` carries region/zone/cluster/device and
the K8s backend maps only `pool` and `region` — so I cannot currently aim an armed run at
`sg8txs64`. Suggestions welcome; otherwise the plan is to keep armed attempts running until one
draws the node.

## Config

Unchanged from the 1-rack recipe in my previous comment: d2048, 22 layers, 128 experts top-4 plus 2
shared, seq 65536, sliding window 2048, `gpu_fa4_cute` + `sonic_cute`, `expert_chunks=1`,
`replica_axis_size=1`, batch 64, `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=0`, on `main` at `d7bddb0ad` plus the `ctxext`
launcher variant.

spillover_issues.body:
Part of #7616

Before the build steps start, the pipeline needs a fixed input and a fixed output shape. Pin which PDFs we read, and agree what a finished document looks like. This gives #7618 to #7621 a stable target.

Pointers:

- The input is the focus crawl `CC-SUPPLEMENTAL-2026-22`, on the public bucket `s3://commoncrawl/projects/cc-open-athena-test/CC-SUPPLEMENTAL-2026-22/`. Object reads are anonymous through the gateway `https://data.commoncrawl.org/...`; only a *list* of the keys may need credentials. [`commoncrawl/crawl-openathena`](https://github.com/commoncrawl/crawl-openathena) [#15](https://github.com/commoncrawl/crawl-openathena/issues/15) and [#18](https://github.com/commoncrawl/crawl-openathena/issues/18) describe the file layout.
- To enumerate the PDF records, the natural options are the Common Crawl [columnar index](https://commoncrawl.org/blog/index-to-warc-files-and-urls-in-columnar-format) (filter on the PDF content type) or the focus crawl's own index. A checksummed manifest of the records is the recommended artifact.
- The output is Marin [`NormalizedData`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2d99584153cb999eb277f627679c410a6b27e2aa/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/normalize.py) (a stable `id`, the `text`, and provenance back to the WARC record). [`focus_crawl.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/20b7003fea217ec031c0cfe77643854641abbffc/experiments/datakit/focus_crawl.py) shows the provenance fields.

Done means: the input is pinned and reproducible, the output shape is agreed with the primary contact (Will Held), and a short note flags the personal-data and copyright risk of PDFs and says the data needs a review before any public release.

comments.author: muchanem
comments.body:
🤖 Input and output are pinned as follows (code in #8023).

**Input.** The crawl-wide columnar index of `CC-SUPPLEMENTAL-2026-22`, filtered to
untruncated 200-response PDFs: 3.16M records across 4,573 WARCs (~4.1 TiB). The plan
step writes a checksummed per-range manifest (one Parquet row per coalesced range,
ordered by task) plus a plan artifact carrying the totals the fetch step commits to.
The whole index must be read even for a sampled run because it is sorted by
`url_surtkey`, scattering each WARC's records across all parts.

**Fetch.** Ranges are coalesced per WARC (1 MiB gap) and packed into 256 MiB tasks:
~686 records/WARC collapse into ~74 ranges, so the full crawl is ~340k range GETs
rather than 3.17M per-record requests. Fetch validates the exact Content-Range,
resumes mid-range across stalls, and hard-fails if any planned record is missing.
The 10% validation sample fetched 411 GiB / 316,297 PDFs; sampling is at range level,
which keeps inclusion probability uniform so the sampled per-task profile matches the
full run.

**Output shape.** Marin `NormalizedData` all the way through. Both extraction routes
emit one record schema (`document_record.PDF_DOCUMENT_FIELDS`): `id` (content hash),
`text`, `source_id` (WARC filename:offset), `source`, WARC provenance, `url`,
`num_pages`, `page_offsets` (per-page character offsets into `text`), extraction
status/diagnostics. The OCR route appends its own diagnostic columns; the combine step
carries them as nullables plus the router's `needs_ocr` decision.

**PR #7917** (shared Common Crawl WARC layer) was evaluated for this step: skipped for
now. It is a strictly per-record client (exactly one record per request, buffered in
RAM), while this fetch's design center is coalesced multi-record ranges — the regime
that suits this PDF-dense crawl (73.5% of crawl bytes). The real shared piece, the
retrying HTTP session, is already shared via `datakit/download/http_session.py`. One
thing #7917 has that we lack is payload SHA-1 verification against the index digest; a
cheap follow-up is a one-off validation pass over the fetched Parquet comparing
`sha1(pdf)` to the stored `content_digest` column.

**Risk note.** PDFs carry sensitive data content at higher density than web text. The
output is for internal training-data research; any public release needs a review first
(FinePDFs ships under ODC-BY for comparison).

comments.author: tinuademargaret
comments.body: This implementation makes sense to me. I’ve updated #7917 to use the same design: coalesce per-WARC ranges, pack them into fetch tasks, and validate every planned record and payload digest. Sparse selections are fetched as individual records through the same path.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
`DataLoaderIterator` retrieves `prefetch_size` training batches through one all-or-nothing `data_store.get_batch(...)` call. It enqueues no result until that call completes. A full queue can hide a producer running below the consumer rate; the consumer then blocks at fetch-window boundaries after the queue drains. This is the mechanism described in [#7012 comment 5007009232](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7012#issuecomment-5007009232), where two data paths reportedly stalled only after their warm prefetch buffers drained.

Reproduce:

```bash
git checkout agent/b200-repro-loader-starvation
uv run --package marin-levanter \
  python lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_loader_prefetch_starvation.py
```

The synthetic backend returns four training batches every 0.4 seconds, for a sustained capacity of 0.1 seconds/batch. Both scenarios start with an eight-batch queue after a 1.3-second warmup.

Observed on both a local CPU and a B200-class accelerator: a consumer requesting one batch every 0.05 seconds drains the queue from eight to zero, then waits about 0.15 and 0.20 seconds at steps 16 and 20 while four-batch bursts arrive. A consumer requesting one batch every 0.125 seconds completes all 24 steps with no waits above 0.1 seconds. The script asserts both outcomes and prints per-step wait time, queue occupancy, fetch windows, elapsed time, and throughput.

The smallest reproduced boundary is `consumer_interval < fetch_delay / prefetch_size`. Increasing `max_buffered_batches` delays the first stall but does not change the sustained-rate boundary.

Expected: a long run should not depend on a finite warm buffer to hide producer underfeeding. Production diagnostics need per-worker fetch latency and queue occupancy so a dataset/backend throughput limit can be separated from storage, network, or slow-worker tail latency.

Claim boundary: this synthetic repro establishes the queue-drain and burst-emission mechanism. It does not attribute the production producer deficit. [#7344](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344) covers a separate collective hang.

Artifacts: [branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/agent/b200-repro-loader-starvation), [commit 23263a8da](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/23263a8da), and [investigation logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/agent/b200-repro-loader-starvation/.agents/projects/20260721_loader_prefetch_starvation.md).

Part of #6710.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The supplied CPU reproduction matches the issue: the faster consumer drains the eight-batch queue and waits at steps 16 and 20, while the sustainable consumer has no waits above 0.1 seconds. `DataLoaderIterator._produce_batches()` builds a full `prefetch_size` window, and `_do_retrieve_batch_of_batches()` flattens that window into one awaited `get_batch()` call, so no result enters `BackgroundIterator` until the whole window completes. Buffer depth only moves the first stall when producer capacity is below consumer demand; current diagnostics report consumer waits above 0.5 seconds and pending fetches above 10 seconds, but not completed-window rate or occupancy.

**Relevant code**
- [`loader.py#L268-L309`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/26f32165e05769f6f30ea5ac81fffac39fc33a19/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/loader.py#L268-L309) - all-or-nothing fetch window
- [`loader.py#L419-L470`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/26f32165e05769f6f30ea5ac81fffac39fc33a19/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/loader.py#L419-L470) - flattened dataset request
- [`loader.py#L249-L261`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/26f32165e05769f6f30ea5ac81fffac39fc33a19/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/loader.py#L249-L261) - consumer stall warning
- [`background_iterable.py#L67-L90`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/26f32165e05769f6f30ea5ac81fffac39fc33a19/lib/levanter/src/levanter/utils/background_iterable.py#L67-L90) - queue consumption and occupancy

# Proposed Diagnostic Change

This telemetry is not a throughput fix. Emit one structured INFO event per completed fetch window on every JAX process with the batch range, batch and item counts, fetch duration, implied batch rate, and queue occupancy before and after the fetch; keep scheduling and exception behavior unchanged. Add a behavior-focused regression for those semantic fields and rerun the supplied starvation benchmark. An instrumented production run must then determine whether ordered concurrent windows, partial-result streaming, or work in Datakit, TreeCache, storage, or networking raises sustained producer throughput; #7474 remains open until that bottleneck is fixed and validated.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Production log check changes the diagnosis:

- Slim: all workers logged one 7.386–8.320s wait before training progress. There were no loader watchdog warnings, and the run then completed 100 steps at roughly 12.1–12.5s/step without another loader stall.
- Datakit: all workers logged one 70.069–76.856s wait before training progress. It then ran 145 steps at roughly 12.0–12.9s/step without another loader stall. The later failure was the separate collective hang tracked in #7344.
- The narrow timing spread across every worker points to a synchronized startup event, not a slow-worker tail.
- At steady state, one 32-batch Datakit fetch took about 73s while consuming those batches took about 390s, so the measured producer had ample sustained capacity.

The current production evidence therefore does not show a steady-state dataloader throughput deficit. The synthetic reproduction is useful for demonstrating what happens when a consumer is intentionally faster than its producer, but that is not the behavior in these production runs.

The production behavior is explained by startup ordering: the training loop creates the iterator and immediately requests batch 1, while DataLoaderIterator withholds all output until its first 32-batch retrieval completes. A candidate behavior change is to retrieve and expose one bootstrap batch first, then use the normal 32-batch windows while the first compiled training step runs. That would address the observed startup latency; it would not claim to increase sustained producer throughput.

#7474 should remain open until we agree whether its intended scope is the observed cold-start latency or a still-unreproduced steady-state throughput problem.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Closing as not planned based on the available evidence.

The synthetic benchmark demonstrates the expected result when a consumer is deliberately faster than its producer: a finite queue eventually drains, and increasing the buffer only delays that point. It does not establish a Levanter throughput defect or identify a production bottleneck.

The cited production claim could not be matched in the available run logs. The inspected Slim and Datakit runs each showed one synchronized wait across workers before training progress, followed by sustained loading without later loader stalls. That evidence supports cold-start latency, not steady-state prefetch starvation.

We should reopen this issue if a production training run shows repeated queue exhaustion after startup. Useful evidence would include the exact run and task IDs, affected training steps, completed fetch-window durations, and queue occupancy over time. First-batch latency can be tracked separately without treating it as a steady-state throughput fix.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Reopening: the sustained-underfeed regime this issue modeled is now visible in production.

The July close was right on July's evidence. The Slim and Datakit runs inspected then each showed one synchronized wait before training progress and no later loader stalls, which is a startup event rather than a throughput deficit. The MoE hero small-scale ablations since 2026-08-14 02:51 UTC show the other regime: repeated stalls at exact fetch-window boundaries, continuing for hundreds or thousands of steps.

`throughput/loading_time` spikes land on step multiples of 32, which is the `prefetch_size` default set in `Trainer.data_loader` and inherited by `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py`. Steady-state step time is 0.42 s, so the producer has ~13.4 s to deliver a 32-batch window; observed stalls of 40 s put it at roughly 3-4x over budget. This is `consumer_interval < fetch_delay / prefetch_size`, the boundary the benchmark on `agent/b200-repro-loader-starvation` established.

Representative runs in `marin-community/marin_moe`:

- Worst observed: [mhep-abl6711-d768-no-latent-norm-20260813-r5](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-abl6711-d768-no-latent-norm-20260813-r5) — 5199 s of `loading_time`, 100 stalls above 0.5 s after step 0, still stalling at step 3712 of 10616.
- Current cohort: [mhep-abl6711-d768-sconv-global-20260814-r6](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-abl6711-d768-sconv-global-20260814-r6) — 1845 s, 28 stalls after step 0.
- Same-day control on the pre-incident store: [mhep-d768-baseline-skipc01-marinpath-20260814](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-d768-baseline-skipc01-marinpath-20260814) — 75 s total, all of it at step 0, no stalls afterward across 10616 steps.
- Store swapped with process topology held fixed at one process per GPU: [ar8062-13-518aec6b83](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ar8062-13-518aec6b83) has 0 stalls after step 0; [ar8062-17b-8e40426cbf](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ar8062-17b-8e40426cbf), same harness and same batch shape on the replacement store, has 22.

Across 303 runs with at least 50 logged steps, grouped by the token store they read:

| store | runs | runs with a stall after step 0 | stalls per run |
|---|---|---|---|
| `marin/slimpajama-6b` | 161 | 0 | 0.00 |
| `marin/datakit/store_8ac06c74` | 108 | 25 | 0.54 |
| `datakit/store_8ac06c74` | 21 | 17 | 17.24 |
| `marin/datakit/store/store_8ac06c74_recompute` | 12 | 12 | 23.08 |
| `.../harrier-all-sources-10m/store/nemotron_0a366c27` | 1 | 1 | 19.00 |

Two cautions on reading that table. Each replacement store occupies a disjoint slice of wall-clock time, so store identity and hour cannot be separated from these runs alone. And severity is not a function of the store: `ar8062-22` and `ar8062-22b` share a commit and a store 36 minutes apart, and record 0 and 11 stalls respectively.

The benchmark still runs unmodified against current `main` and both assertions hold, so the harness needs no repair: the faster consumer stalls at steps 16 and 20 with the queue at 0, and the sustainable consumer completes 24 steps with 0.003 s of total wait.

Buffer depth is being tried as a mitigation, and this issue already covers why that is not sufficient: increasing `max_buffered_batches` delays the first stall without moving the sustained-rate boundary. Production behavior agrees, with stalls persisting past step 3700 in the worst run.

The diagnostics gap called out in the original report is unchanged. A representative run logs 513 metric keys and none come from tensorstore, so `loading_time` remains the only record. tensorstore already exports what is needed, confirmed present in the installed 0.1.84 binary: `/tensorstore/kvstore/s3/retries`, `/tensorstore/http/response_codes`, `/tensorstore/kvstore/s3/read_latency_ms`, and `/tensorstore/kvstore/s3/bytes_read`. All are readable in-process through `ts.experimental_collect_matching_metrics("/tensorstore")`. Logging them alongside `loading_time`, together with the `BackgroundIterator.qsize()` occupancy this issue's script already reads, would separate a storage throughput limit from client-side backoff and would measure read amplification directly.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correcting the reopen: this is a decaying warm-up transient, not a sustained underfeed.

The 2026-08-14 comment above described a sustained regime, quoting `consumer_interval < fetch_delay / prefetch_size` and citing a run "still stalling at step 3712 of 10616". That reading does not survive a look at the full history of the same runs. Every affected run pays a large cost at consecutive fetch-window boundaries, the cost decays monotonically, and then it stops completely.

| run | store | spikes | first → last spike | mean, first → last third | after the last spike |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mhep-abl6711-d768-no-latent-norm-20260813-r5` | `store_8ac06c74_recompute` | 100 | 32 → 3712 | 85.0 s → 25.3 s | 6905 steps, max 0.000 s |
| `rav-ladder-d768-v2` | `store_81e7e39a` | 55 | 32 → 1856 | 81.3 s → 7.7 s | 9564 steps, max 0.357 s |
| `rav-ladder-d768-v2-old-mix` | `store_8ac06c74_recompute` | 24 | 32 → 2048 | 87.0 s → 20.5 s | 9372 steps, max 0.000 s |
| `rav-ladder-d2048-v3` | `store_81e7e39a` | 6 | 64 → 224 | 60.4 s → 29.2 s | 13344 steps, max 0.000 s |
| `ii2r-l1-20260807-165117` | `slimpajama-6b` | 0 | — | — | 20000 steps, 0.3 s total |

Every spike in every run lands on a step that is a multiple of 32, without exception, which is the `prefetch_size` window boundary. The run cited as evidence of persistence spikes 100 times and then logs 6905 consecutive steps at exactly zero.

So the July close was closer to correct than the reopen allowed. What July underestimated was the scale, not the kind: this is not one synchronized startup wait but roughly one hundred window-boundary waits decaying over about 3700 steps, which is long enough to read as steady state if only the early part of a run is inspected. It also means `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_loader_prefetch_starvation.py` on `agent/b200-repro-loader-starvation` models the wrong regime. It constructs a consumer that is permanently faster than its producer, and production does not show that.

Two things the reopen got right and that still justify keeping this open. The cost is large: 4909 s on the worst run, 2029 s and 1145 s on the two d768 ladder rungs. And the all-or-nothing fetch window is what turns a per-first-touch cost into multi-minute blocking stalls instead of spreading it across steps.

The store correlation reported earlier also needs narrowing. Old and new datakit stores behave the same, so the August rebuild is not the variable: `store_8ac06c74_recompute` and `store_81e7e39a` both warm up over roughly two thousand steps. What separates them from `slimpajama-6b` is layout, not vintage. The datakit stores are sharded-layout caches with 168 to 200 mixture components; slimpajama is a single consolidated component and logs no spike across 20000 steps.

A decaying first-touch cost is what a lazily opened per-shard tensorstore produces, and on the sharded read path the shard open was the only per-shard network first touch. `_ensure_shard_field_offsets` resolves from `field_counts_by_shard` in the ledger with no I/O, so it does not contribute. #8333 makes those opens concurrent rather than serialized on the loader's event loop; whether that accounts for most of the warm-up is not yet measured against a real store, and tensorstore's own cache pool amortizes on the same curve.

Separately, and not covered by this issue: on 2026-08-18 both a hero-scale d2048 rung and several small-scale runs show MFU dipping at every prefetch boundary while `loading_time` is at zero, so there is a second cost at the same period that this metric cannot see. `loading_time` only measures time the consumer spends blocked in `next()`, and the producer thread stacks and transfers all 32 batches back to back once a window lands. That deserves its own issue rather than more history here.

spillover_issues.body:
Issue to track tokens per second of all candidate architectures at the 15B-30B active scale, using our best effort hardware tuning. These will serve as data points from which we can interpolate to select our training run.

Top candidates:

- [99 days for 20T tokens](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5054192424). MuonH · d6144 · 4-of-256 experts · 48 layers — ~707B total / ~22.6B active — 2-rack FSDP.
- [82 days for 20T tokens](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5036748495). MuonH · d6144 · 4-of-128 experts · 48 layers — 359.6B total / 22.6B active
- [120 days for 20T tokens](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201#issuecomment-5060285897). MuonH · d6144 · 4-of-128 · MLA + full-width 72-head attention + learned relative-position bias — ~360B total / ~21.3B active. (slowdown is from no sliding window, poor relative position kernel, and 1.5x heads). This can be tuned further and needs more quality validation.

I am estimating (may heavily update after floppy phoenix), that we will want to allocate 80 days for pretrain, -10 days for hardware, - 3 days for earlier cooldowns, -4 days for long context penalty. This gives 63 days for expected pretrain. This would put option one at 12.7T tokens, option 2 at 15T tokens, and option 3 at 10.5T tokens. Improving MFU will let us train on more tokens in this window.


Each comment should include a branch link, wandb link, iris job link, MFU, tokens per second, batch size, and training duration. One comment per architecture option, that gets updated over time as MFU on it improves. If training on 1 Rack, project out to 12 racks with 12x batch size and 7% slower tokens/second/rack. (initial estimate based on architecture test with first comment, may not hold with higher parameter counts)

Examples of items to test:
Replica Scale: replicate after 16, 32, or all 64 GPUs.
Batch size: When do we run into memory pressure
FSDP vs EP: can we get aware with pure FSDP still
Adam vs Muon speed, memory and step time dynamics.
scaling total experts from 64->128->256. Consider impact on memory and speed for both FSDP vs EP, and Muon vs Adam.
Alternating dense/MoE, what change in tokens per second
Impact of MTP on TPS
Impact of MLA on TPS
Impact of expert granularity on TPS (4/64 -> 8/128, 4/256 -> 8/512)
Impact of Latent MoE on TPS (may need more efficient EP kernel to get meaningful numbers here)
Longcat-style parallel MoE path to hide all-to-all
Longcat2 engram embedding
Remat policy.
FP8 Impact.

Command A+ (Cohere, May 2026)
From the HuggingFace config: it's a decoder-only sparse MoE with a SigLIP vision encoder attached, and 218B total / 25B active parameters. MoE: every layer is MoE — first_k_dense_replace: 0, so there is no dense/MoE alternation at all. 128 experts with 8 active per token, sigmoid expert selection with normalized top-k. MAI-Thinking-1 / MAI-Base-1 (Microsoft AI, June 2026)
A 35B-active / 1T-total sparse MoE trained from scratch on 8K GB200 GPUs. From Table 1 of the tech report (the MAI-Base-1 row): [Microsoft](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/mai-thinking-1.pdf)

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **MLA vs GQA — 1-rack throughput sweep (GB200, 64 GPU)**

Threw the full MLA (DeepSeek-V3-style Multi-head Latent Attention) sweep against the GQA baseline on a single GB200 rack. Every run is the **same d5120 / e128 model**, differing only in the attention block, so tok/s is directly comparable.

Branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/b200_mla

Shared config: d5120 · 48L · 128 experts top-4 (+1 shared) · intermediate 2560 / shared 5120 · sliding window 2048 (3:1 short:long) · seq 4096 · batch 1024 · MuonH+SYRK · sonic_cute MoE · FA4-CuTe attention · 64 GPU. MLA: `kv_lora_rank=512`, `q_lora_rank=2048`, decoupled RoPE (qk = qk_nope + qk_rope).

**MFU is intentionally omitted** — the MFU model-FLOP formula assumes standard attention (hidden/heads) and does not account for MLA's compressed-latent projections or asymmetric head dims, so it isn't comparable across MLA and GQA. Tokens/sec (median of per-step history) is the honest metric.

| Attention config | heads | full q width | full v width | tok/s | vs baseline |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| MLA · qk128 · 1× | 40 | 5,120 | 5,120 | **333,601** | +0.8% |
| **Baseline GQA (hd128, 40h/10kv)** | 40 | 5,120 | 5,120 | **330,958** | — |
| MLA · qk192 · 1× | 40 | 7,680 | 5,120 | 316,351 | −4.4% |
| MLA · qk128 · 2× | 80 | 10,240 | 10,240 | 277,873 | −16.0% |
| MLA · qk192 · 2× | 80 | 15,360 | 10,240 | 255,329 | −22.9% |
| MLA · qk256 / v256 · 1× | 40 | 10,240 | 10,240 | 42,936 | −87.0% |

`full q width = heads × (qk_nope + qk_rope)`, `full v width = heads × v_head_dim`. qk128 = 64+64, qk192 = 128+64, qk256 = 192+64; v_head_dim is 128 except the last row (256). 1× = 40 heads (d/head_dim), 2× = 80.

<details><summary>runs</summary>

- MLA qk128·1×: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d5120-64gpu-r1-e128top4-mla-kv512-q2048-qk128-h1x-slim-30
- Baseline GQA: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d5120-64gpu-r1-e128top4-gqa-baseline-slim-30
- MLA qk192·1×: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d5120-64gpu-r1-e128top4-mla-kv512-q2048-h1x-slim-30
- MLA qk128·2×: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d5120-64gpu-r1-e128top4-mla-kv512-q2048-qk128-h2x-slim-30
- MLA qk192·2×: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d5120-64gpu-r1-e128top4-mla-kv512-q2048-slim-30
- MLA qk256/v256·1×: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d5120-64gpu-r1-e128top4-mla-kv512-q2048-qk256-v256-h1x-slim-30

</details>

Human summary:
MFU is cratering at head dim 256, will avoid. Matching head dims, MLA is roughly neutral on throughput. The convention with MLA is to heavily increase the head count and run at higher q and k head dims (192). This increases the quadratic attention flops. So you end up with higher training flops per parameter, and heavier penalty for longer training sequence length. 

The viable space here looks to be qk192 (qk128 will likely do poor on loss), then we vary head count between 1x and 2x, taking on a 4-20% training slowdown at 4k seqlen. This will likely grow to a 2x slowdown at 64k seqlen. Early results [wandb report](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/64xH100-Hardware-Validation-Run-and-MLA-Test--VmlldzoxNzQ3MDExNw) indicate that head count at 2x w/ MLA is only giving a 8% quality boost, compared to GQA baseline. Unlikely this compensates for the 1.2-2x slowdown it will incur during training. It is surprising that the quality boost is so low. 

I will kick off a large number of ablations in the MLA space, to see if the 8% quality gain can be improved. I would expect closer to 20% quality gain is possible, given the flop overhead of 2x heads. That would make it an easier decision to include. 

Quality Ablations: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7374

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **MuonH · d6144 · 4-of-128 experts · 48 layers — 359.6B total / 22.6B active — FSDP chunk-2 MoE**

(Chunk 2 functions similarly as EP=2 in terms of token dropping)

Same d6144 architecture as the earlier hidden_dim-6144 push, now with the **chunked-expert FSDP MoE** overlap: the routed expert-weight all-gather is split into 2 chunks so chunk *k*+1's gather hides under chunk *k*'s QuACK GEMM. On the fastest config (sw512 / 8-KV / local:global 5:1) this lifts throughput from **245.9K tok/s @ 21.8% MFU** (single unchunked all-gather) to **253.0K tok/s @ 22.7% MFU**.

**Architecture**
- Optimizer: **MuonH** (Newton-Schulz on 2D/3D/4D matrices incl. the scanned 4D `[L,E,in,out]` expert stacks; GatedNorms on Muon, RMSNorm/embed/router/lm_head on Adam)
- Routing: **top-4 of 128 experts** (+ 1 always-on shared expert)
- **48 layers**, **hidden_dim 6144** (48 heads / **8 KV (6:1)**, head_dim 128), expert intermediate 3072, shared-expert 6144, **512 sliding window**, **local:global 5:1** (every 6th layer full-causal), long-rope off
- **Total params: 359.6B** (routed experts 347.9B) · **Active params: 22.6B** (top-4/128, excludes embedding + lm_head)
- **MoE impl: `sonic_cute` with `SCALE_MOE_EXPERT_CHUNKS=2`** — dispatch runs once, then each of the 2 expert-chunks all-gathers only its half of the FSDP-sharded expert weights and runs the QuACK grouped GEMM over its token segment, so the second gather overlaps the first chunk's compute.

**Throughput (GB200, FSDP + intra-rack sharding, muonh, sonic_cute chunk-2 MoE, FA4 CuTe attn)** — 12-step probe, 1 rack (64 GPUs), batch 1024, SlimPajama:

| | GPUs | batch | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 rack (measured)** | 64 | 1,024 seq × 4096 (4.19M tok/step) | **253.0K** | **22.7%** |
| **12 racks (projected, −7% weak-scaling)** | 768 | 12,288 seq × 4096 (50.3M tok/step) | **~2.82M** | **~21.1%** |

**Training duration: 20T tokens → ~82 days** at 12 racks.

Measured = p50 MFU over the steady steps of the probe (p50 22.71%, mean 22.77%, p10/p90 22.64/23.13, tok/s 252,958; tight σ 0.16). The 12-rack projection applies the standard 7% weak-scaling penalty (1-rack tok/s × 12 × 0.93); 20T duration = 20e12 ÷ 12-rack tok/s. Chunking is the one FSDP-overlap lever that lands at this scale — replicating or prefetching attention weights across the scan either OOMs (activation replication) or hits the #7407 CUBIN load bug at d6144.

**Exact Iris submission command** (chunks=2; `WANDB_API_KEY` passed from env, never expanded):

```bash
uv run iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --enable-extra-resources \
  --target-cluster cw-us-east-08a --priority interactive \
  --cpu 2 --memory 8GB --disk 32GB --timeout 5400 \
  --job-name gb200-d6144-64gpu-embshard-chunks2-profile-coord \
  -e SCALE_GPUS_PER_NODE 4 -e SCALE_GPU_TYPE GB200 -e SCALE_GPU_REPLICAS 16 -e SCALE_EXPERT_AXIS 1 -e SCALE_REPLICA_AXIS 1 \
  -e SCALE_HIDDEN_DIM 6144 -e SCALE_NUM_LAYERS 48 -e SCALE_NUM_KV_HEADS 8 -e SCALE_NUM_EXPERTS 128 -e SCALE_TOP_K 4 \
  -e SCALE_SEQ_LEN 4096 -e SCALE_SLIDING_WINDOW 512 -e SCALE_GLOBAL_EVERY 6 -e SCALE_BATCH 1024 -e SCALE_STEPS 12 \
  -e SCALE_DATA slimpajama -e SCALE_OPTIMIZER muonh \
  -e SCALE_MUON_DIST_NONEXPERT 1 -e SCALE_MUON_INTRA_RACK 1 -e SCALE_MUON_PAD_NONEXPERT 1 -e SCALE_MUON_SYRK 1 \
  -e SCALE_WATCH_INTERVAL 20 -e SCALE_MOE_IMPL sonic_cute -e SCALE_ATTN_IMPL gpu_fa4_cute -e SCALE_SCAN_LAYERS 1 \
  -e CE_IMPL liger -e CE_LIGER_CHUNK 8192 -e SCALE_REMAT recompute_all -e XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR cuda_async \
  -e SCALE_MOE_EXPERT_CHUNKS 2 \
  -e SCALE_TRACKER wandb -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" -e WANDB_PROJECT marin_moe \
  -e RUN_ID gb200-d6144-64gpu-embshard-chunks2-profile \
```

- wandb: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d6144-64gpu-embshard-chunks2-profile
- Iris job: https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Flarry%2Fgb200-d6144-64gpu-embshard-chunks2-profile-coord


---

**Update — full-feature model @ 4-of-128, enabled by host offloading**

the one throughput lever added is **host offloading** (`SCALE_OFFLOAD_OPT_STATE=1`): park the MuonH optimizer state (~22 GB/GPU, dominated by expert momentum, idle through fwd/bwd) on **pinned host memory**, freeing the HBM the memory-bound scheduler needs to overlap the backward weight re-gathers. Viable on GB200 via the ~900 GB/s Grace↔Blackwell NVLink-C2C link (the round-trip hides under the ~15 s step; it would lose on a PCIe host).

**1 rack (64 GPUs), batch 1024, chunk-2:**

| config | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---|---|
| chunk-2 ( above) | 253.0K | 22.7% |
| **full-feature + host offload** | **255.3K** | **23.1%** |

**12 racks (projected, −7% weak-scaling):** 768 GPUs → **~2.85M tok/s @ ~21.5% MFU**. **Training duration: 20T tokens → ~81 days** (255.3K × 12 × 0.93; 20e12 ÷ 2.85M tok/s) — vs ~82 days for chunk-2.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correction and apples-to-apples EP1 result (2026-07-21)

The earlier 108.4K MXFP8 result should not be compared with the published EP1 BF16 result: those runs differed in expert parallelism and backend/config details. I have caveated the earlier comments.

I reran a same-source, same-config pair on 64 GB200 GPUs. Both arms used d6144/L48/E128/top4, EP1 (FSDP only), the same batch/data/optimizer, FA4 attention, ring/current scatter MoE dispatch, scan, Liger CE, rematerialization, and the branch's current fixes/optimizations. The only treatment change was `SCALE_FP8=mxfp8` with the XLA producer. MXFP8 wire communication remained disabled (`wire: null`).

Median rank-0 throughput over steps 2–29 (28 samples per arm):

| Compute path | Median tok/s | Relative to BF16 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| BF16 | 187,502 | 1.000× |
| MXFP8 | 140,351 | 0.749× |

On this EP1 implementation, enabling MXFP8 reduced end-to-end throughput by 25.15% (BF16 was 1.336× faster). This result does **not** show that MXFP8 tensor-core arithmetic itself is 25% slower: it includes quantization/cast/lowering and kernel-path overheads. It also does not include reduced wire communication, so communication savings are not masking the result here.

Both runs completed all 30 training steps with finite, decreasing loss, then failed while writing the disposable local final checkpoint. That post-training failure did not affect the measured window. This is one run per arm, so treat the size of the gap as exploratory pending profiling or replication.

Source base: `c3cb334f8ede1967cf42cf69e61a705d65bbc11e`; identical local patch in both arms: `50f1c595af02df2338c0beb908acb0c7c23f054a499cd0b45169fc1af0878307`.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **MuonH · d5120 · 8-of-256 experts · 48 layers — 249B total / 14.5B active — EP64 ragged all-to-all MoE**

The **expert-parallel** counterpart to the FSDP-chunk path above: instead of replicating/gathering the expert weights (EP1 + FSDP), this shards the 256 experts across a **64-wide expert axis** (one NVLink domain = 1 rack) and routes tokens with `ragged_all_to_all`. This is the regime for *many* experts where the weights can't be gathered, and it pays an all-to-all tax the FSDP path doesn't: `ncclDevKernel_SendRecv` (dispatch + combine) is **~28% of GPU time** and is the dominant MFU limiter. Current result: **~13% MFU** typical.

**Architecture**
- Optimizer: **MuonH** (Newton–Schulz on 2D/3D/4D incl. the scanned 4D `[L,E,in,out]` expert stacks; SYRK on)
- Routing: **top-8 of 256 experts** (+ 1 always-on shared expert), capacity factor 1.0
- **48 layers**, **hidden_dim 5120** (40 heads / **10 KV (4:1)**, head_dim 128), expert intermediate 1280, shared-expert 5120, **2048 sliding window**
- **Total params ~249B** (routed experts 241.6B) · **Active ~14.5B** (top-8/256, excl. embed + lm_head)
- **MoE impl `ragged_all_to_all`** — permute → ragged a2a dispatch → grouped GEMM → ragged a2a combine, all over the intra-rack `expert` axis (NVLink, never IB)

**Fixes required to run at EP64** (each is load-bearing — without it the run OOMs before the first step)
1. **MuonH 4D Newton–Schulz OOM** (`optim/grugmuon.py`) — the `(L,E)→LE` merge declared `PartitionSpec(None,"data","model")`; under EP (`data=model=1`) that fully replicates the `[L·E,D,I]` bf16 stack on every device — **~300 GiB at L48, observed OOM 310 GiB** — before the reshard can redistribute it. Fix: transpose the `expert` axis to the front so each shard's slice stays contiguous and the merge lands in an expert-sharded spec with no gather. No-op at EP1/FSDP.
2. **Non-expert FSDP sharding** (`grug/sharding.py`, `moe/model.py`) — `data = devices/(replica·expert)`, so EP collapses `data` to 1 and every **non-expert** weight (attention, shared-MLP, lm_head) **and its optimizer state** replicates on all devices — **~148 GiB/GPU at d5120/L48, OOMs before step 1**. Fix: `Pfsdp = ("data","expert")`, shard those weights `P(Pfsdp, "model")` / `P("model", Pfsdp)`. `expert` is intra-rack so the all-gather stays on NVLink; identical to `P("data",…)` at EP1.
3. **Flash attention** (`SCALE_ATTN_IMPL=gpu_fa4_cute`) — the FA4 CuTe SM100 kernel; replaces reference attention that materialized the `bf16[batch,heads,seq,seq]` score matrix (~80 GiB) and lifted MFU **~10.5% → ~13%**.
4. **Env-driven capacity factor** (`SCALE_CAPACITY_FACTOR`, default 1.0) — receive capacity = `capacity_factor × tokens_local × topk`; watch `train/router/capacity_overflow_rate_mean`.

**Throughput (GB200, EP64, muonh, ragged_all_to_all, FA4 CuTe attn)** — 1 rack (64 GPUs), batch 1024, 12–24 step probe:

| | GPUs | batch | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 rack (typical)** | 64 | 1,024 seq × 4096 (4.19M tok/step) | **~212K** | **~13.0%** |
| 1 rack (best observed) | 64 | same | 261K | 16.9% |

Measured = p50 MFU over steady steps (typical run p50 12.7–13.2%, tok/s 208–216K). **Caveat: the same config swings to ~16.9% purely on node placement** — one run hit p50 16.2% / 261K tok/s, and a direct repro landed back at 13.5% — so ~13% is the honest number and single-run A/Bs here are placement-noisy. The gap to the FSDP-chunk path's 22.7% is the all-to-all: at EP64 the dispatch/combine SendRecv is ~28% of the step and is not yet overlapped.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **MuonH · d6144 · 4-of-256 experts · 48 layers — ~707B total / ~22.6B active — 2-rack FSDP, full-feature + host offload**

Scaling the routed pool to **256 experts** (2× the 4-of-128 above) and **sharding the model across 2 racks** (128 GPUs, FSDP over `data`), carrying the full training feature set (**GatedNorm + attention gate + XSA + QB routing**) with **host offloading** of the MuonH optimizer state to pinned host memory.

**Architecture**
- Optimizer: **MuonH** (Newton-Schulz on 2D/3D/4D matrices; distributed NS with QuACK SYRK)
- Routing: **top-4 of 256 experts** (+ 1 always-on shared expert), **QB** (DeepSeek-V3 aux-loss-free) balancing
- Features: **GatedNorm** (post-RMSNorm), **per-head attention gate** (2·sigmoid, zero-init identity), **Exclusive Self Attention (XSA)**
- **48 layers**, **hidden_dim 6144** (48 heads / **12 KV**, head_dim 128), expert intermediate 3072, shared-expert 6144, **512 sliding window**, local:global 5:1, long-rope off
- **Total params: ~707.5B** (routed experts 695.8B) · **Active params: ~22.6B** — unchanged from 4-of-128, since top-k is fixed at 4 and only the pool doubled
- **MoE impl: `sonic_cute` chunk-4** (`SCALE_MOE_EXPERT_CHUNKS=4`, 64 experts/chunk — finer gather/compute overlap; the best config at 2 racks, see below); **host offloading** `SCALE_OFFLOAD_OPT_STATE=1` (opt-state parked on pinned host between steps → HBM freed for the memory-bound scheduler; GB200 NVLink-C2C)
- **Sharding: FSDP over `data=128` across both racks** (`SCALE_REPLICA_AXIS=1`) — 2 experts/GPU, same per-GPU density as the 1-rack 4-of-128

**Throughput (GB200, 2 racks / 128 GPUs, batch 2304, SlimPajama, 12-step probe)**

Cross-rack FSDP is comm-bound; two levers help — larger batch (amortize the InfiniBand weight-gathers; knee ~16–18 seq/GPU) and finer MoE chunking (more gather/compute overlap):

| config | batch | seq/GPU | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| chunk-2 | 1,024 | 8 | 265K | 12.0% |
| chunk-2 | 2,048 | 16 | 387K | 17.5% |
| chunk-2 | 2,304 | 18 | 402K | 18.1% |
| **chunk-4** | **2,304** | **18** | **412K** | **18.6%** |

Best = **chunk-4 @ batch 2304: 18.6% MFU / 412K tok/s** (p50 18.63, mean 18.66). Chunk-4 adds **+0.5 pt** over chunk-2 at the same batch — finer chunking hides more of the cross-rack expert-weight gather.

**12-rack / 20T projection**

| | GPUs | batch | tok/s | MFU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **2 racks (measured)** | 128 | 2,304 seq × 4096 (9.4M tok/step) | **412K** | **18.6%** |
| **12 racks (projected)** | 768 | 13,824 seq × 4096 (56.6M tok/step) | **~2.35M** | **~17.7%** |

**Training duration: 20T tokens → ~99 days** at 12 racks (20e12 ÷ 2.35M tok/s). The projection scales the measured 2-rack tok/s by 6× and applies a **~5% weak-scaling penalty for 2→12 racks** — not the 7% used for 1→12 elsewhere: the big cross-rack hit is **already** in the 2-rack number, so 5% (≈ 7% × log₂6 / log₂12) is just the incremental degradation over the smaller 6× span.

The **cross-rack penalty is the dominant cost**: the same full-feature model is ~23% MFU on 1 rack (4-of-128) vs ~18.6% here (4-of-256, 2 racks) — the drop is FSDP weight-gathers + Muon stack reshards crossing the InfiniBand rack boundary instead of NVLink.
